source.title: Non-asymptotic Analysis of Expected Reconstruction Risk for Trigonometric Polynomial Models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper is present, though some mathematical notation is garbled in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests the sample-size version through expected reconstruction risk versus the number of samples. In the equidistant and small-jitter settings it reports declining risk and a drop at the interpolation threshold, rather than an increase in risk as more samples are added. It also shows that the outcome depends on the sampling scheme.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double-descent work, but cited findings are not recorded. Its results concern reconstruction risk in trigonometric polynomial regression, not test error in deep networks. The uniformly random-sampling results establish divergent expected risk at fixed m and N, not how risk changes as m increases. The reported sample-size sweeps for equidistant and jittered sampling are relevant to V3.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps sample count m across the interpolation threshold m = N at fixed model size N for min-norm least-squares trigonometric regression. Because the Fourier basis is orthonormal, coefficient reconstruction risk equals the function's L2 test error. This is a new, non-deep-network setting with a sample-wise result bearing on V3. In the equidistant and small-jitter designs, risk falls monotonically through the threshold with no peak. The paper does not argue against double descent, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors also frame the m = N behaviour as a phase transition with a sudden risk drop, not a peak, and do not claim to test double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes least-squares reconstruction for trigonometric polynomial models using Fourier–Vandermonde sampling matrices and expected squared reconstruction risk, rather than measuring deep-network test error against model size, epochs, or data size.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on the sampling scheme: independent uniform sampling has divergent expected risk, while equidistant and sufficiently small jittered sampling show a transition and declining risk. The paper also reports that the upper bound for jittered sampling is loose below the threshold when m is close to N.

fits_no_version.finding: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling (and jitter of width 1/m), expected least-squares risk is infinite at fixed m and N. Rare near-colliding nodes make 1/σr² heavy-tailed (Hill α̂ ≈ 0.20 at m = 33, N = 41).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In random-design min-norm regression, expected risk can be dominated or made infinite by ill-conditioned rare designs, independent of the m/N ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: Whether a sample-wise peak appears depends on the smallest singular value of the design. A well-conditioned equidistant design removes the peak entirely.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak at m = N requires an ill-conditioned design near the threshold; well-conditioned sampling eliminates it.

record.problems: The reported sweeps concern reconstruction risk in trigonometric polynomial regression rather than deep-network test error. The paper provides no uncertainty intervals for the numerical curves. The upper bound for jittered sampling is reported to be loose when m < N and m is near N; the independent-uniform divergence result does not compare risk across sample counts.

untested.parts: Model-wise curve; N is fixed within each sweep and no deep networks are studied.
Epoch-wise curves; the estimator is closed-form least squares.
Deep networks, and designs with non-trivial conditioning near m = N under finite expected risk.
Label-noise or regularization dependence of a peak, and multiple peaks; no regularization or noise-level sweep is reported.

missing.what: Jittered-sampling risk curves with Theorem 15 lower and upper bounds. The lower bound tracks the empirical risk, while the upper bound inflates (axis up to 1e14) near m→N from below, which is a bound artifact rather than an empirical peak.

record.verdict_notes: V3's states are changed from reversed to absent, because a monotone decrease is the ordinary behaviour and V3's effect (a rise) is simply missing. Labels are limits_scope rather than challenges because V3 says more data 'can' hurt, and these are specific well-conditioned designs. The noise level ε and Monte Carlo counts for Fig. 1 are not stated.

versions.untested_parts: Model-wise test-error curve in deep networks.
The study measures expected reconstruction risk, not deep-network test error; it does not establish a rise in risk with increasing sample count. Its uniform-random results are at fixed m and N.
Capacity-wise double descent across model classes.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across axes.
Noise or regularization dependence of a peak, multiple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Whether counting effective parameters turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Fourier–Vandermonde matrix A (equidistant sampling)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep the number of equidistant sampling points m and report expected reconstruction risk.
rows.value: Theorem 10: Nϵ²/m² for m ≥ N; ((m + N − 2b)/(a(a + 1)m²))ϵ² + N − m for m < N, where N = am + b. The text says risk decreases before the threshold, drops sharply at m = N, and then decays smoothly.
rows.note: The paper reports a theoretical formula and describes the numerical curve as decreasing with a sharp drop near the interpolation threshold; it does not report a rise as m increases.
rows.check: V3's effect is a rise in error with more samples near m = N. Theorem 10 gives risk ≈ N−m plus a small variance term for m<N and Nε²/m² for m≥N, so risk only falls. That is no rise, not an opposite effect, so the state should be absent rather than reversed. Fig. 3 shows empirical averages over 1000 noise draws matching the formula. The noise level ε is not stated.

relationships.reason: Exact risk (Theorem 10, Fig. 3) falls monotonically through m = N with no rise. Here more samples never hurt, so V3 depends on design conditioning (R1, R2).
